sections.text: Moving values in and out of every function would be tiring. Instead you can lend a value with a reference, written with &. This is called borrowing.
The function gets a reference, uses it, and gives it back automatically. The owner keeps the value, so word is still usable afterwards.
You can have as many shared references (the Book and compiler errors call them immutable references) as you like at the same time, because nobody can change the value through them:

A reference must never outlive the value it points to. The compiler checks this, so Rust can't have dangling pointers. The commented-out dangle function below doesn't compile: it tries to return a reference, but there's no value that lives long enough for it to borrow from:
A reference is like letting a friend read your book while you watch. They give it back, and you still own it.
The part of the compiler that enforces this is the borrow checker. In idiomatic code, parameters usually take &str rather than &String; you'll see why in the Slices lesson.

exercise.prompt:
Change total_length to borrow both Strings instead of taking ownership, so main can still print a. It should print: 9
good

tests.label: total_length of "good" and "night" is 9
Both Strings are still usable afterwards

hints: Passing a String to a function moves it. Change the function so it only borrows both of them.
Use & in two places: before String in each parameter type, and before each variable in the call.
Write x: &String and y: &String in the function. In main call total_length(&a, &b). The tests call total_length(&a, &b) the same way, so pass references, not clones.

quiz.question: What does &word create?
quiz.explanation: &word creates a reference: it borrows word and lets you read it without taking ownership, so word is still usable afterwards. A copy would need .clone(), and the owner stays the same.

quiz.question: How many shared (&) references can exist at once?
quiz.explanation: Any number of shared (&) references can exist at the same time, because reading doesn't cause conflicts. The limits only start when something wants to change the value.

quiz.question: Why can't a function return a reference to its own local String?
options: The String is dropped when the function ends
quiz.explanation: A local String is dropped when the function ends, so a reference to it would point at memory that is already freed. Rust refuses to compile this. You can return references in general, as long as the value lives long enough, and you can also return the String itself.
